opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm genuinely optimistic, though I try to be specific about where I think the acceleration will actually come from.

Over the next five to ten years, I think the biggest shift is that AI moves from being a tool scientists use for isolated tasks, like predicting a protein structure or classifying cell images, to something closer to a research collaborator. In my group we've been experimenting with what we call virtual labs, where teams of AI agents take on different scientific roles. One agent acts like an immunologist, another like a computational biologist, another plays a critic. They discuss a problem, propose hypotheses, write and run code, and design experiments. In one project, that kind of setup helped design nanobodies against new SARS-CoV-2 variants, and when we tested them in the wet lab, a good number of them actually worked. What struck me was less any single prediction and more that the whole cycle, from idea to candidate to experiment, compressed dramatically.

So the first area is speed of iteration. A lot of science is bottlenecked not by lack of ideas but by how long it takes to explore a hypothesis space, read the literature, set up analyses, and decide what's worth testing. AI agents can do much of that exploration in parallel and around the clock.

The second area is integration with automated experimentation. Generative models for proteins, small molecules, and even cell states are getting quite good. The real leverage comes when you close the loop: the model proposes, a robotic or high-throughput lab tests, and the data flows straight back into the model. As those loops get tighter, I expect real gains in areas like protein engineering, antibody design, and functional genomics.

The third area, which I think gets less attention, is that AI can help us make better use of data we already have. There's an enormous amount of underused biomedical data: clinical records, single-cell atlases, published figures, even social media discussions among pathologists, which we used to build pathology foundation models. Turning that messy knowledge into something models can learn from is itself a form of discovery.

I'd add a few caveats. Biology is still fundamentally constrained by the physical world. You can generate a million candidate molecules overnight, but validating them, especially in humans, takes time, and clinical trials won't shrink by a factor of a hundred. So I expect the most dramatic acceleration early in the pipeline, in hypothesis generation, design, and preclinical work, and more modest gains downstream unless we also rethink trial design and regulation.

There's also the question of reliability. These systems can be confidently wrong, and in science that's dangerous because a plausible but false result can send people down the wrong path for years. A lot of my thinking now is about evaluation: how do we audit AI-generated hypotheses, how do we make sure agents report uncertainty honestly, and how do we keep humans meaningfully in the loop instead of just rubber-stamping outputs.

Overall, I think in five to ten years many labs will routinely work alongside AI agents that propose and critique ideas and run analyses, and the distinctive human role will move toward choosing the right questions, setting priorities, and exercising judgment about what really matters. If we get the validation and incentives right, I think we could see a real step change in the pace of discovery, especially in biology and medicine.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI models proposing designs that robotic or high-throughput labs test, with results fed back into the models, and says this closed loop will drive gains in scientific areas such as protein engineering and antibody design.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I'm genuinely optimistic, but I want to be precise about where the optimism comes from, because I think the popular picture of "AI will discover new drugs" gets the mechanism slightly wrong.

The way I think about it is that science has a few distinct bottlenecks, and AI is going to hit them very unevenly. The first is generating hypotheses and reading the literature. Here I think the progress is already real. We've been building what we call AI scientist or virtual lab systems in my group, where you have multiple language model agents taking on different roles, a principal investigator, an immunologist, a computational biologist, a critic, and they actually meet, argue, and design experiments together. When we did this for nanobody design against new SARS-CoV-2 variants, the agents proposed candidates that we then validated in the wet lab, and a couple of them bound the variants. So that loop, from idea to experimental design, is getting dramatically cheaper. A good graduate student can now explore ten or twenty times the hypothesis space they could before.

The second bottleneck is the physical experiment itself, and that's where I think people overestimate the near-term speed. Cells still take days to grow. Mice still take months. Clinical trials still take years and they're governed by biology and regulation, not by compute. So even if you have a perfect model of the hypothesis side, you're still rate-limited by the world. The interesting question for the next five to ten years is whether automated labs and better simulation can shrink that loop, and I think they will partially, especially for things like protein design, where the design-to-test cycle is already fast, and for cell-level perturbation experiments where you can run thousands in parallel.

The third bottleneck is one people talk about less, which is evaluation. How do you know an AI-generated finding is actually right? Language models are very good at producing plausible-sounding science, and plausibility is exactly the wrong thing to optimize for in research. So a lot of our work is on building rigorous benchmarks and on having these systems be honest about uncertainty. I think that is going to determine whether the acceleration is real or whether we just flood the literature with confident-sounding noise.

If I had to put a number on it, I'd say over the next decade the rate of credible hypothesis generation and analysis goes up by an order of magnitude or more, the rate of confirmed biological discovery maybe doubles or triples, and the gap between those two numbers is going to be the defining tension of the field. The scientists who do best will be the ones who treat these systems as very fast, very well-read collaborators that still need a skeptical human running the lab.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI systems making hypothesis generation and experiment design cheaper, alongside automated labs and better simulation that can speed experimental loops in areas such as protein design and cell perturbation. It presents their convergence as an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery.

astra-6.text:
I’m very optimistic, especially if we think of AI as part of the scientific process rather than just a tool for answering questions. In biotechnology, we can generate enormous amounts of data, but turning that data into a useful hypothesis—and deciding which experiment to run next—is still a major bottleneck. AI has the potential to help at each of those steps.

The really exciting possibility is a tighter loop between computation and experiments. A model proposes a candidate molecule or a biological mechanism, we test it, and the results help the model make a better proposal. Over the next five to ten years, I think we could see those loops become much more effective, allowing researchers to explore possibilities that would otherwise be too expensive or time-consuming to investigate.

But I would distinguish accelerating discovery from accelerating the delivery of a treatment to patients. Biology is complex, and a promising computational prediction still needs experimental validation. Safety, clinical trials, and manufacturing remain substantial challenges. Progress won’t be equally fast across all of those stages.

So my optimism is less about AI suddenly solving biology and more about giving scientists much greater capacity to ask and test good questions. If we can pair better models with reliable experiments and learn from the failures as well as the successes, that could meaningfully change the pace of discovery.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI models proposing biological candidates, experiments testing them, and results improving later proposals, creating a more effective discovery loop and new opportunities to explore.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m very optimistic, especially because AI can help close the loop between generating hypotheses and testing them. In biology, we can measure an enormous number of things, but turning those measurements into a useful experiment is still difficult. AI can help identify patterns, propose explanations, and prioritize which experiments are most informative.

Over the next five to ten years, I think the biggest gains will come from connecting these models more tightly to experimental biology. A model could propose a protein or a potential therapeutic, researchers could test it, and those results could inform the next round of predictions. That iterative process could substantially accelerate discovery.

But we should distinguish generating promising candidates from demonstrating that they actually work. Biology is complicated, and a prediction that looks compelling computationally may fail in a real biological system. So the opportunity is tremendous, but realizing it requires good experiments, careful validation, and models that can recognize when their predictions are uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response connects AI models with extensive biological measurement and experimental testing, describing an iterative process that could accelerate scientific discovery.
